titolo: DISSIPATE No. 8 OF NINE NEVADA DEPRESSIONS
testo: Five shallow trenches lined with wood, cut into the dry lakebed of Black Rock Desert in Nevada and placed as if matches had been dropped on the ground. Part of a series of nine works across the Nevada desert, made to be eroded and lost. Land art at its beginning: sculpture made by taking material away.

A huge boulder hangs above a stormy sea, with a small castle growing out of its top. Magritte paints the impossible with the calm precision of a postcard, so that gravity seems to be the thing that is wrong. The painting is in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

A single gridded structure that wraps the whole planet, crossing deserts, cities and seas without changing. The Florentine group drew it in collages as a critique of architecture's will to order everything. One of the founding images of Radical Architecture.

A single plate of hot-rolled steel, eight by twenty-four feet, wedged into the corner of a room and held there only by the two walls. It cuts the space in two, and as you walk around it the plate turns from surface to edge and back. Now at the Guggenheim, New York.

An extinct volcanic cone in the Painted Desert of Arizona, bought by Turrell in 1979 and reshaped from inside into an observatory for the naked eye. Tunnels and chambers frame the sky, the sun and the moon. Still in progress after more than four decades.

titolo: The Elemental House, the California Pool
testo: A 1950s ranch house reworked around the four elements, earth, water, air and fire. Its pool is shaped like the State of California. Postmodern symbolism, played with a straight face.

An open lattice of identical square cells, the same in every direction. LeWitt chose the cube because it is the least expressive form there is, and so it lets the system be the subject. The idea is the machine that makes the art.

With Paul Virilio, Parent proposed living on inclined planes instead of flat floors: walking would become climbing, and the body would feel every move. Built examples are few, the church of Sainte-Bernadette in Nevers (1966) among them, but the drawings remain.

A small city for children: repeated domed units grouped in clusters, with interior streets and courtyards between them. Van Eyck called it a house like a small city and a city like a large house. A founding work of Dutch Structuralism.
Painted in his last years at the Bauhaus in Dessau: thin, floating geometric shapes on a black ground. For Kandinsky black was a silence without future, against which every color sounds sharper.

An endless, homogeneous interior, lit and air-conditioned like a supermarket, where furniture and tents replace buildings. Archizoom drew it with a typewriter, as a grid of characters, to show the city as pure quantity. A radical critique of the modern metropolis.
A white dove with spread wings, suspended in formaldehyde inside a glass and steel case. The sign of the Holy Spirit and of peace becomes a specimen.
A monochrome canvas opened by clean cuts with a blade. Fontana's slashes are not destruction but an opening onto the space behind the painting. 'Attese' means waitings.

A floating wooden theatre built for the Venice Biennale, towed across the lagoon on a barge and moored in front of the Punta della Dogana. It belonged to the city for one season, then it was dismantled. Rossi's most poetic building, made to disappear.

From the series of Still Lifes begun in 1962: collage and paint on board, with supermarket products and advertising images arranged like a Dutch still life. American abundance seen in the flat language of the billboard.

German pavilion for the International Exposition in Barcelona: free-standing walls of onyx and green marble, chromed cruciform columns, and a reflecting pool. Demolished in 1930 and rebuilt on the same site in 1986.
Lichtenstein quotes Matisse's goldfish bowl and translates it into Ben-Day dots, black outlines and flat color. Painting about painting, in the language of comic strips.

titolo: “The Big Duck”, Long Island, New York
testo: A building in the shape of a duck, built by a duck farmer to sell ducks and eggs. Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown and Steven Izenour used it in Learning from Las Vegas (1972) as their 'duck': a building whose form is its sign, against the 'decorated shed'.

Bayer studied at the Bauhaus in Weimar and in 1925 became head of the new printing and advertising workshop in Dessau. He designed the 'universal' alphabet in lower case only. Typography reduced to geometry.

Ghirri was born in Scandiano, near Reggio Emilia, and began photographing in the early 1970s, while still working as a surveyor. His Emilia is made of signs, walls and empty corners, looked at with quiet attention.

Hayakawa built his architecture around the 'landscapes that architecture produces' in the city. His Tokyo houses read like fragments of stage set, layered planes and colors in a dense, fragmented city.
A drawing from Learning from Las Vegas: a plain shed with a huge sign that announces 'I am a monument'. The decorated shed, where the meaning is written on the building rather than built into it.
The Drawbridge: stairs, bridges and walkways climb through a vast, impossible prison. The Carceri were first etched around 1745–50 and reworked, darker and deeper, in 1761.

OMA's competition entry for a park on the site of the old Paris slaughterhouses: the ground cut into parallel strips, each one a different programme, laid side by side like the floors of a skyscraper turned on its side. The competition was won by Bernard Tschumi, but the strips became one of the most copied diagrams in architecture.

An old drum factory turned into a leisure centre, kept almost as it was found. Next to it, two concrete towers joined by flying walkways, with windows like holes torn in the walls. Bo Bardi called it a citadel of freedom.
A city reduced to a few lines, blocks and signs, somewhere between a map and a piece of music. Klee taught at the Bauhaus until 1931 and drew cities as if they were written.

A housing block on a corner of Kreuzberg, built for the IBA. Its long curved façade follows the street without a single gesture of style. Someone painted 'Bonjour Tristesse' on the roof parapet, and the name stayed.

A cemetery garden for the Brion family, with pools, a chapel and an arched shelter over the graves. Two interlocking circles in the wall look onto the fields. Scarpa is buried here, just outside the walls.
Gorin met Mondrian in Paris in the 1920s and spent his life carrying Neo-Plasticism into relief: primary colors, black lines and white planes that step forward from the wall.

Part of the ceiling Michelangelo painted between 1508 and 1512. God reaches toward Adam, who lifts his hand lazily back; between the two fingers, a gap of a few centimetres that holds the whole image.
A wall of silkscreened mouths, taken from a publicity still of Marilyn Monroe and repeated until the face disappears. Made in the months after her death in August 1962. Hirshhorn Museum, Washington.
LaChapelle photographed wax figures of celebrities and politicians after they were damaged in transport: broken heads, faces cracked open. Fame turned into a pile of fragments.

The story of a Rio de Janeiro favela from the 1960s to the 1980s, told by a boy who becomes a photographer. Shot with many non-professional actors from the favelas, it moves at the speed of the violence it shows.

Namuth photographed Pollock painting in his barn studio in Springs, Long Island, moving around a canvas laid on the floor. These photographs and Namuth's film turned the act of painting into the image everyone remembers.

From the series 'Salvataggi di centri storici': Florence filled with water up to the cupola of the Duomo, which stands out of the lake like an island. Made a few years after the real flood of 1966, as an ironic proposal to 'save' the city.
A boy wanders through the ruins of Berlin after the war. Shot on location among the bombed buildings, it closes Rossellini's war trilogy after Roma città aperta and Paisà.

A lithograph in which Escher holds a mirrored ball and draws himself reflected in it, with his whole room curving around him. The artist always stays at the centre of the sphere, whichever way he turns.
A day in a Soviet city, filmed without actors, script or intertitles. Vertov and his editor Elizaveta Svilova show the camera, the cameraman and the editing table as part of the film itself.
A 28-minute film made almost only of still photographs. A man is sent back from a ruined Paris to a memory of a woman on the observation pier at Orly. In one single shot, she moves.

Three concrete slabs, six thin columns and a stair: a frame for houses to be built quickly after the war. Walls no longer carry anything, so plan and façade become free. The skeleton of modern architecture.

A household falls apart while the mother sleeps: a child smokes, a dog eats the pie, a pig wanders in with the tap. The title is a Dutch proverb, and every detail is a moral warning painted with obvious pleasure.

A film without words: landscapes, cities, crowds and machines, slowed down or sped up, set to the music of Philip Glass. The title is a Hopi word for 'life out of balance'. Cinematography by Ron Fricke.
A film director who cannot make his film, caught between memories, women and producers. Fellini turned his own creative block into the film, and ended it with everyone holding hands in a circle.

titolo: Old Man Looking Through the Window
testo: A man leans out of a painted window, so precisely rendered that the frame seems to be part of the wall. Hoogstraten, a pupil of Rembrandt, was a master of trompe-l'œil and of perspective boxes.
Antonioni's American film, made in the desert of Death Valley. It ends with a villa exploding again and again in slow motion, and everything it held, clothes, food, books, floating in the sky.

Three movements in which the performer plays nothing. At its first performance in Woodstock, the pianist David Tudor opened and closed the lid of the piano to mark them. The music is whatever sound happens in the room.

titolo: First Flight of a Commercially Built Airplane

testo: One of the 'blackboard' paintings: loops of white line run across a grey ground like handwriting on a school slate, repeated until they become a current.

titolo: TV Murder in a Hotel on the Croisette
testo: A staged scene in a hotel room in Cannes: fashion photography that borrows the look of a crime still. Newton made glamour cold, theatrical and slightly dangerous.

A photographer with a broken leg watches the courtyard of his building in Greenwich Village and becomes convinced that a neighbour has committed a murder. The whole film was shot on one huge set, a cross-section of windows.

titolo: The Waters of Lethe by the Plains of Elysium
testo: Souls in white robes walk down to the river of forgetting before entering paradise. A painting of the second Pre-Raphaelite generation, close to Burne-Jones in its long figures and pale light.

titolo: Unknown - from the Dirty Windows Series
testo: From a friend's apartment, Alpern photographed through the bathroom window of a club in Lower Manhattan. Grainy, cropped by the window frame, the pictures make the viewer a voyeur too.
Peasants bring eggs and chickens as payment to a lawyer buried in paper. Brueghel the Younger painted many versions of this scene, a satire on bureaucracy that sold well then and still works.
A love letter to New York shot in black and white by Gordon Willis, set to Gershwin. The best-known image: two figures on a bench at dawn, under the Queensboro Bridge.
The inside of a discount supermarket in Los Angeles, photographed from above and digitally reworked so that every shelf is equally sharp. Abundance becomes an abstract pattern.

Built for Italia '61, the exhibition for the centenary of Italian unity. The huge square hall is covered by sixteen independent umbrellas: a concrete column that opens at the top into a crown of steel ribs.

From Arbus's last series, photographed at Halloween parties and picnics in residences for people with intellectual disabilities. Masks, costumes and open fields; the photographs were printed after her death.

titolo: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
testo: 2,711 concrete blocks of different heights on a sloping field near the Brandenburg Gate. Walking in, the ground sinks and the blocks rise above your head: a place without a centre, where you lose the others.
From Le Antichità Romane, Piranesi's four volumes on the ruins of ancient Rome. The plan of the city becomes a fragment of stone itself, drawn as if it were carved and broken.

The militia company of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, painted not standing in rows but in the middle of moving off. A girl lit up in gold and the captain's hand reaching out are the brightest points in the shadow.
From 'Changing New York', Abbott's survey of the city in the 1930s. Every inch of the restaurant front is covered in hand-painted prices and dishes: a façade made of words.
A porcelain urinal, turned on its back and signed 'R. Mutt'. Submitted to an exhibition that was supposed to accept everything, and refused. The original was lost; the art world never recovered.

From the Principia philosophiae: the space around a magnet drawn as a field of swirling particles, threaded through the earth. A diagram of an invisible force, almost two centuries before Faraday's field lines.

titolo: The City of the Captive Globe
testo: A grid of blocks, each one a different ideology built as a tower, with a globe suspended at the centre. Later published in Delirious New York (1978), Koolhaas's 'retroactive manifesto' for Manhattan.
The Corleone family, from the wedding in the garden to the closing door. Gordon Willis lit it so darkly that he was nicknamed 'the Prince of Darkness': faces emerge from shadow as in an old painting.

titolo: A Sudden Gust of Wind (after Hokusai)
testo: A large lightbox photograph restaging a print by Hokusai in a field near Vancouver. It looks like a single instant, but it was assembled from many photographs taken over months.

titolo: Wanderer Above the Sea of Fog
testo: A man seen from behind stands on a rock above a sea of fog. We see what he sees, and we cannot see his face. The image of the Romantic individual in front of nature.
The first map to use the name 'America', given to the new lands in honour of Amerigo Vespucci. Printed in twelve sheets; the only known surviving copy is in the Library of Congress.

titolo: Studies for the Seven Heavenly Palaces
testo: Kiefer's seven towers of stacked concrete containers were built in 2004 in a former factory in Milan, now Pirelli HangarBicocca. The name comes from the Sefer Hechalot, a Hebrew mystical text about the ascent to heaven.
Three men share a cell in a New Orleans prison, then escape through the swamps of Louisiana. Black and white photography by Robby Müller, with Tom Waits, John Lurie and Roberto Benigni.

A wooden theatre in which the spectator stands on the stage and looks at the seats, where the whole of knowledge is arranged in images. Camillo described it in L'idea del theatro, published in 1550; the theatre itself was never completed.
The Infanta Margarita and her ladies-in-waiting, Velázquez at his canvas, and in the mirror at the back the king and queen. The painting looks at us from the place where the royal couple stands.
Models covered in Klein's patented blue paint pressed their bodies on paper, while musicians played his 'Monotone-Silence Symphony'. The body became a living brush.
A television set with a large magnet placed on top: moving it bends the electron beam and turns the picture into abstract shapes. One of the first works of video art.
A cable TV programmer discovers a signal that changes the bodies of those who watch it. Television becomes flesh, and the screen breathes.
It opens with a woman beating a man, and her wig coming off. A former prostitute tries to start again in a small town that hides much worse. Fuller's B movie, as hard as a headline.

titolo: Vanitas Still Life with a Jewellery Box, Skull on a Reversed Crown, a Globe, and a Lute
testo: A skull on an overturned crown, a globe, a lute and a jewellery box: wealth, power, knowledge and music, all passing. Collier, active in Leiden, London and Amsterdam, painted many vanitas around 1700.
Children drawing on the street in Prospect Place, Brooklyn, seen from above. Leipzig photographed New York's street games for years, a world of play now gone.

Sea and sky, divided exactly in the middle by the horizon, photographed with long exposures in many seas of the world. Each one looks the same and each one is different: water and air, as the first humans saw them.
A triptych: Eden on the left, hell on the right, and in the middle a garden full of naked figures, giant fruit and strange buildings. Closed, its shutters show the world in a glass sphere.
Dalí curled up as an embryo inside an egg, an image made with Halsman to illustrate Dalí's claim that he remembered life before birth. The start of a collaboration that lasted thirty years.

The bedroom Loos designed for his wife Lina: white fur on the floor, white linen draping the walls and the bed. A room almost without architecture, all softness and light, from the man who wrote against ornament.

titolo: The Alluvial Valley of the Lower Mississippi River
testo: Maps drawn for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, showing the old courses of the river in colored bands, one over the other. A geological survey that looks like a painting.
A spiral of black basalt and earth, 460 metres long, running into the red water of the lake. It disappeared under the water for decades and reappeared white with salt.
A hollow sphere 150 metres high: by day, small holes in the vault turn the inside into a night sky; by night, a lamp inside becomes the sun. An architecture for an idea, never meant to be built.
A man sits alone with his glass, and the green fairy appears on the table before him. The painting has hung for more than a century in the Café Slavia, facing the Vltava.
A twelve-year-old boy works as a scout on the Eastern Front. Tarkovsky's first feature cuts from the war to his dreams of light, water and his mother. It won the Golden Lion in Venice.

Built in the garden city of Hellerau for Émile Jaques-Dalcroze's school of rhythmic movement. Inside, an empty hall with walls of white fabric lit from behind, designed with Alexander von Salzmann and Adolphe Appia, a space for bodies and light.
A huge drawing for a painting never finished: the deputies of the Third Estate swearing, in June 1789, not to separate until France had a constitution. The wind blows the curtains into the room.
The lessons of the most influential architecture teacher of eighteenth-century Paris, published in nine volumes of text and plates. Boullée and Ledoux were among his students.
Two women by the pool of Richard Neutra's Kaufmann House in Palm Springs. Aarons spent his life photographing 'attractive people doing attractive things in attractive places'.
The philosophers of antiquity gathered under a vast vaulted hall, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre. Raphael gave Plato the face of Leonardo and painted himself at the edge, looking out at us.
The cinema Kubelka designed for Anthology Film Archives: all black, with each seat hooded and screened on the sides, so that the viewer saw only the film and nothing else.
A drawing of a New York with streets on several levels: cars below, pedestrians on arcaded walkways above, and bridges between towers.
A linguist is asked to learn the language of visitors who write in circles of ink. As she learns it, her memory of time changes. Cinematography by Bradford Young.
Friedlander built his pictures out of the clutter of American streets: reflections, signs, poles and his own shadow crossing the frame, so that nothing stays in front of anything else.
A cone cut through two seventeenth-century houses about to be demolished next to the site of the Centre Pompidou. For a few weeks, passers-by could look through the buildings to the sky.
Asked for a portrait of James Joyce, Brancusi drew a spiral and three lines. It was published in Joyce's Tales Told of Shem and Shaun.

titolo: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
testo: Hunter S. Thompson's book on screen: a journalist and his lawyer cross the desert to Las Vegas in a convertible full of drugs. The carpets and walls of the casinos come alive.
Ferdinand leaves his life in Paris and runs away to the south with Marianne. Primary colors, comic strips, painted faces and the Mediterranean: Godard's road movie ends with dynamite.
Ghirri returned again and again to the small towns of Emilia, where he was born. Billboards, painted walls and empty horizons, photographed in pale color as signs to be read.

A 'laboratory of fun' that would never be finished: a steel frame with cranes that move rooms, floors and screens according to what people want to do. Never built, but the Centre Pompidou owes it a great deal.
A boat carries a figure in white toward a rocky island with cypresses. The first of five versions Böcklin painted; Rachmaninoff wrote a symphonic poem after it.
A young man in Paris becomes a pickpocket almost as a philosophy. The thefts are filmed like a ballet of hands, with non-professional actors Bresson called 'models'.
Marco Polo describes to Kublai Khan fifty-five cities, each with a woman's name. Perhaps they are all Venice. A book about cities, memory and desire that architects never stopped reading.
Fontana photographed the landscapes of Emilia as fields of pure color, flattened by the light into lines and planes. A photography close to abstract painting.
An actress stops speaking; a nurse takes care of her on an island, and talks for both. Their faces end up merging into one. Cinematography by Sven Nykvist.
Pier Vittorio Aureli and Martino Tattara's answer to Archizoom's No-Stop City: a city made of a few huge, identical slabs set in an open field. Limiting the city instead of letting it spread.
Renoir's friends having lunch on the balcony of the Maison Fournaise on the Seine, near Chatou. Among them is Aline Charigot, holding a dog, whom he later married.
1982 was Basquiat's most prolific year: skulls, crowns, words and anatomy painted at speed, in the language of the street.

From 'Unconscious Places', Struth's black and white photographs of streets in Europe, Japan and the United States, taken from the middle of the road at a calm distance. The city as it is, without event.
Three chapters of a diary: Rome in August on a Vespa, the Aeolian islands, and an illness. The ride ends at the place in Ostia where Pasolini was killed.
A zinnia grown on the International Space Station, photographed by Scott Kelly in January 2016. It grew in NASA's Veggie experiment, after the plants had almost died of mould.

A square for the Italian community of New Orleans: columns of every order in stainless steel and neon, fountains, and a map of Italy in stone running into a pool. Postmodernism in its most theatrical form.
The life of the eighteenth-century Armenian poet Sayat-Nova told in tableaux: almost still images of carpets, books, pomegranates and faces. The Soviet censors re-edited it and changed its title.

titolo: Plan for the Reform and Expansion of Barcelona
testo: The plan that extended Barcelona beyond its walls with a grid of blocks with cut corners. Cerdà also wrote the first general theory of urbanisation.
Han Youngsoo photographed Seoul in the years after the Korean War. On the island in the Han River, small figures cross a wide space of snow and light.
An orange nylon curtain 381 metres wide, hung across a valley in the Rocky Mountains. It stood for 28 hours before a gale forced its removal.

titolo: Steel Beams and Lots of Danger
testo: A worker crouched on the end of a steel beam high above Victoria Harbour, wrench in hand. The city at his feet was growing upwards.
D'Arcangelo painted the American road as the driver sees it: the asphalt, the signs and the line of the horizon reduced to flat color and hard edges.
A truck pours a load of hot asphalt down the slope of a quarry outside Rome and lets it run. Sculpture as an act of entropy.

An ideal cross-section of the earth's crust, from Heinrich Berghaus's Physikalischer Atlas, compiled from the work of Nöggerath, Humboldt, Cotta and others. Mountains, volcanoes and strata in one imaginary landscape.
The last of five paintings on the rise and fall of an imaginary empire. Here nothing is left: a column covered in ivy, ruined bridges and the moon over the water.
Max, the painter of 'Cosmic '60s' pop, made landscapes in thick strokes of color: water, reeds and sky, the same view repeated through the seasons.

Born in the sea off Naples in 1950, Parthenope crosses decades of the city's beauty and decay. Sorrentino films Naples the way he films his heroine: sunlit, theatrical, always slightly out of reach. Cinematography by Daria D'Antonio.
